rows.title: 1.5 million Ram pickups recalled over software problem affecting stability control
rows.standfirst: Stellantis is recalling nearly 1.5 million Ram pickup trucks worldwide to fix a software problem that can disable the electronic stability control system.

rows.title: Summer camp capitalism
rows.standfirst: Summer camp is a classic rite of passage in the U.S. It's a place of self-discovery, where kids come to make new friends and take on new challenges. But what if it were ALSO a place where children came to learn how to survive in a free market economy?

rows.title: U.K. is investigating Ticketmaster after Oasis tour prices surprised fans
rows.standfirst: British regulators are looking into how Ticketmaster uses "dynamic pricing" to hike prices in line with demand. A similar controversy prompted a federal lawsuit against the company in the U.S.

rows.title: Why aren't more people taking on the trades?
rows.standfirst: There is expected to be a lot of demand for manufacturing jobs in the coming decade, but many of those positions will be left unfilled. So Darnell Epps set out to close that gap by connecting employers with workers and showing potential workers what's appealing about these jobs. Today, we dig into Darnell Epps journey through both law school and trade school.

rows.title: The latest jobs data provides a really confusing picture. Here are 4 things to know
rows.standfirst: There was both good news — and bad news — in the latest jobs report, providing an unclear picture as the Federal Reserve weighs how much to cut interest rates.

rows.title: Red Lobster off the hook? Federal judge approves restructuring plan
rows.standfirst: The restaurant chain announced Thursday that it received approval for its Chapter 11 plan, offering a glimmer of good news for the business, which has faced a series of struggles.

rows.title: NPR listeners share their best money-saving grocery store tips
rows.standfirst: Check your receipt. Grow your own veggies. Ask about senior discounts. NPR readers share their top tips on cutting costs at the grocery store.

rows.title: Trump staffers in cemetery scuffle named. And, dad of alleged school shooter arrested
rows.standfirst: NPR confirmed the names of the two Trump staffers involved in the Arlington cemetery scuffle. And, the father of the Georgia school shooting suspect arrested.

rows.title: Telegram founder breaks silence, calling charges 'misguided'
rows.standfirst: The tech billionaire breaks his silence more than a week after being indicted by French authorities. He faces wide-ranging charges including complicity to distribute child abuse images and to traffic drugs.

rows.title: How Pitbull got his name on a college football stadium
rows.standfirst: Recently, singer/rapper/entrepreneur Pitbull agreed to pay $6 million to Florida International University for the naming rights to its football stadium ... an unusual move for both parties: a musician paying for their name on a stadium, and for a college to name their stadium after a musician .

rows.title: Could you give up shopping for a year? Try the 'no-buy challenge'
rows.standfirst: The goal is to save money, cut back on overconsumption and be more mindful of wasteful and unsustainable shopping habits. This guide can help you start a challenge of your own.

rows.title: The FDA is probing tampon safety after a study found toxic metals in popular brands
rows.standfirst: The FDA says it has commissioned a lab study and a literature review to evaluate metals in tampons, after a recent study found heavy metals like lead in products by over a dozen popular brands.

rows.title: How Russian operatives covertly hired U.S. influencers to create viral videos
rows.standfirst: Details in an indictment match Nashville-based Tenet Media, which offered lucrative paychecks to prominent right-wing influencers. The influencers say they were deceived.

rows.title: Bingo! (Presidential debate edition)
rows.standfirst: Campaigns can be a jargony slog. And this year, we are seeing a lot of economic terms being thrown around, many of which... aren't entirely straightforward.

rows.title: Economic Lingo Bingo: Finally, a way to make a confusing election… fun!
rows.standfirst: The team at Planet Money turned the economics terms being tossed out during the 2024 presidential campaign into a game of Economic Lingo Bingo!

rows.title: FDA approves some Apple AirPods to be used as hearing aids
rows.standfirst: An upcoming Apple software update will allow some AirPods to double as over-the-counter hearing aids. Only 1 in 6 American adults with hearing loss wears hearing aids.

rows.title: The return of Fyre Festival and other indicators
rows.standfirst: It's ... Indicators of the Week! We roundup the economic indicators that caught our attention. On this (kinda) spoOoOooky Friday the 13th, we were morbidly curious about higher household incomes, a Keurig K-Cup kerfuffle and, believe it or not, the return of Fyre Festival.

rows.title: Rate Expectations: What it means that the Fed is about to lower interest rates.
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates to get inflation under control. One side effect is that taking out a mortgage to buy a home has gotten very expensive. That's especially a problem for some homeowners who managed to get a lower mortgage rate years ago. They have a sort of... champagne problem. Or, "golden handcuffs" as it's called.

rows.title: Shein and Temu face a big change to how they ship cheap Chinese goods
rows.standfirst: New White House rules would close a tax loophole that lets Shein and Temu cheaply ship from China to American shoppers. The Biden administration says it undercuts U.S. workers, retailers and manufacturers.

rows.title: China is raising its retirement age, now among the lowest in world's major economies
rows.standfirst: In an effort to address its shrinking population and aging work force, over 15 years, China will raise the retirement age for men to 63, and for women to 55 or 58 years depending on their jobs.

rows.title: Union autoworkers won big after striking. A year later, some face an uncertain future
rows.standfirst: Last fall's strike against Ford, GM and Stellantis yielded record contracts for autoworkers. With a slowdown in car sales, Stellantis workers now face job cuts, production slowdowns and uncertainty.

rows.title: Boeing machinists go on strike after rejecting contract
rows.standfirst: The deal would have raised wages by 25%, lowered employees’ share of health care costs, and boosted retirement contributions by the company. But many rank and file union members were unhappy.

rows.title: The DOJ's case against Apple
rows.standfirst: The Department of Justice thinks Apple has violated an antitrust law, pointing to its ecosystem of apps and products. Apple, for its part, thinks the DOJ is wrong on both the facts and the law. Today on the show, why the DOJ brought this lawsuit against one of the largest companies in the world and why it matters for all you smartphone owners out there.

rows.title: Navient reaches $120 million settlement for misleading student loan borrowers
rows.standfirst: According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, $100 million will be used to make payments to impacted borrowers in a settlement with the former servicer of student loans.

rows.title: After more than a century, the Campbell's company drops 'soup' from its name
rows.standfirst: The Campbell Soup Company's CEO said the "subtle yet important change" to the name adopted in 1922 better reflects the broad number of products it makes.

rows.title: Keurig misled the public over claims its K-Cup pods are 100% recyclable, the SEC says
rows.standfirst: Keurig agreed to pay $1.5 million in penalties — without admitting guilt or denying the SEC's findings that the K-Cup pod producer made inaccurate claims regarding the recyclability of those pods.

rows.title: Overtourism ho! The Barcelona cruise dilemma
rows.standfirst: Barcelona has always attracted crowds, but now it's attracting protests from locals angered at the negative consequences of being one of Europe's most popular destinations. This is especially true as large cruise ships can dock close to some of the city's most famous landmarks. On today's show, we look at how cruise ships are both driving revenues and frustrations in Barcelona, and we consider what the city's options are for regulating the flow of visitors.

rows.title: Is AI overrated or underrated?
rows.standfirst: Are the promises made by AI boosters all hype, or are we actually under-appreciating the transformative potential of AI?

rows.title: A venture capital grant program for Black women officially ends after court ruling
rows.standfirst: Attorneys representing conservative activist Edward Blum and the Atlanta-based Fearless Fund wrote that both parties “have settled,” asking the court to permanently dismiss the case.

rows.title: What Musk's Twitter takeover could tell us about a possible government appointment
rows.standfirst: After buying Twitter in 2022, Elon Musk instituted sweeping changes — including rebranding the social media platform as "X." Authors Kate Conger and Ryan Mac recount the takeover in Character Limit.

rows.title: FTC sues insulin middlemen, saying they pocket billions while patients face high costs
rows.standfirst: The Federal Trade Commission said pharmacy benefit managers created a "perverse drug rebate system" that artificially inflated the cost of insulin.

rows.title: FBI agents board Baltimore ship linked to Singaporean company sued in bridge collapse
rows.standfirst: FBI agents boarded a vessel managed by the same company as the cargo ship that caused the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge in March.

rows.title: The Fed cut rates ... now what? (featuring: Sasquatch)
rows.standfirst: It's ... Indicators of the Week! We roundup the economic indicators that caught our eyes and ears. This week, all our attention was on the Federal Reserve, which cut interest rates by half a percentage point. (Egad!)

rows.title: Without immigrants, America's job growth would have stalled
rows.standfirst: Springfield has become a lightning rod in a pitched battle over immigration. Meanwhile, Dayton has welcomed immigrants for more than a decade, to fill vacant jobs and revitalize old neighborhoods.

rows.title: How to save 10,000 fingers
rows.standfirst: Table saws are extremely dangerous. The government estimates that injuries from table saws send something like 30,000 people to the emergency room every year. 3,000 of those end in amputations. The costs of those injuries are enormous. Are they also avoidable?

rows.title: Philip Morris sells asthma inhaler company, citing ‘unwarranted opposition’ to its goals
rows.standfirst: Three years ago, the cigarette giant acquired Vectura, a British pharmaceutical firm that makes asthma inhalers, raising health groups’ ire. Now, it’s selling the business for almost $200 million.

rows.title: Three Mile Island nuclear plant will reopen to power Microsoft data centers
rows.standfirst: Three Mile Island, the Pennsylvania power plant that was the scene of the worst commercial nuclear accident in American history, will reopen and sell power to Microsoft.

rows.title: Magazine writer Olivia Nuzzi is on leave over an alleged relationship with RFK Jr.
rows.standfirst: New York Magazine said Nuzzi's relationship with a former subject violates its conflicts of interest standards. She said the relationship "was never physical," but apologized for not disclosing it.

rows.title: What are Harris' economic plans?
rows.standfirst: Yesterday we looked at Donald Trump's key economic proposals for a second term. On today's show, we do the same for Kamala Harris, examining the Democratic nominee's plans for taxes, housing and grocery store prices.

rows.title: FAA investigating cabin pressure problem that injured passengers aboard Boeing plane
rows.standfirst: The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating an incident aboard a Delta flight in which a cabin pressurization issue with the Boeing 737 caused some passengers to bleed from the nose and ears.

rows.title: Truth Social reaches a tricky milestone. Will Donald Trump cash out his stake?
rows.standfirst: Trump can now start selling his majority stake in the Truth Social parent company, as a lockup on insider sales expires. But that could tank the price of the stock.

rows.title: In a major shift, the U.S. government explores giving renters cash, not vouchers
rows.standfirst: Federal housing vouchers are the largest rental aid program, but many landlords reject them. Experiments will test whether cash helps more people sign a lease.

rows.title: Here are 4 ways the Federal Reserve's big rate cut could change the housing market
rows.standfirst: Here's a look at what the Federal Reserve's rate cut will mean for those looking to buy — or sell — a home.

rows.title: What are Trump's economic plans?
rows.standfirst: With less than two months before election day in the U.S., there's still a lot to learn about both major candidates' economic platforms. Today we look at some key proposals from Donald Trump for a second term, including tariffs and immigration. Tomorrow: Kamala Harris' plans.

rows.title: Can money buy happiness?
rows.standfirst: People often say that money can't buy you happiness. Sometimes, if you ask them to tell you more about it, they'll mention a famous 2010 study by Nobel Prize winners Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton. That study found that higher household income correlates with greater emotional well-being, but only up to around $75,000 a year. After that, more money didn't seem to matter.

rows.title: Mail bag! Grad jobs, simplified branding and central bank independence
rows.standfirst: Penny for your thoughts? Today we open our mail bag to hear from Indicator listeners. A college graduate tells us about their job search, a researcher discusses why products advertised as 'simple' may not be so straightforward, and another listener thinks the debate over Fed independence is a little more nuanced than we let on.

rows.title: A tiny town just got slammed by Helene. It could massively disrupt the tech industry
rows.standfirst: Spruce Pine is a major global supplier of high-purity quartz. It's an essential ingredient for microchips and solar panels.

rows.title: Amazon India workers say they're overworked and mistreated during a brutal heat wave
rows.standfirst: Amazon India says it ensures breaks and worker safety, but workers tell NPR they're pressured not to stop for water or to use the toilet, especially while processing same-day orders.

rows.title: California Gov. Newsom vetoes AI safety bill that divided Silicon Valley
rows.standfirst: The measure, known as SB 1047, was one of the nation’s most far-reaching regulations on the booming AI industry. It would have held AI companies legally liable for harms caused by AI and enabled a "kill switch" if systems went rogue.

rows.title: Why the price of eggs is on the rise again
rows.standfirst: The price of eggs has risen by about 28% in the past year, largely due to outbreaks of avian flu. Those prices could continue to climb during the holidays, as demand for baked goods increases.

rows.title: What's THAT got to do with economics?
rows.standfirst: "Wanna see a trick? Give us any topic and we can tie it back to the economy."

rows.title: America's small GDP bump, China's big stimulus dispersal, and a Monkey King
rows.standfirst: It's time for ... Indicators of the Week! It is our show where we talk about fascinating numbers from the news. On today's episode, America's small GDP increase, a big assist from China's government to its lower income residents, and a high-grossing, centuries-old Monkey King.

rows.title: East and Gulf Coast dockworkers could strike tonight. Here's what's at stake
rows.standfirst: Some 25,000 dockworkers at East and Gulf Coast ports may strike just after midnight on October 1 if their union doesn't reach a contract deal with shipping companies and port operators.

rows.title: Voting-tech company settles with right-wing network over false election claims
rows.standfirst: Smartmatic sued Newsmax for defamation over false claims related to the 2020 presidential election. The trial was supposed to begin next week.

rows.title: What does the next era of Social Security look like?
rows.standfirst: Peak 65 is here. More than 4 million Americans will turn 65 each year between 2024 and 2027, representing the largest retirement surge in history. Years ago, older Americans could count on Social Security. But today there is some uncertainty on the program's solvency in the next decade plus. Now, many are entering their golden years with financial insecurity. Today on the show, how did Social Security become a thing? And what could the safety net for the Peak 65 generation and beyond look like?

rows.title: Why Russia's broadcaster RT turned to covertly funding American pro-Trump influencers
rows.standfirst: RT was long known to be a source of Russian propaganda. But a recent indictment of two employees for covertly funneling $10 million to pro-Trump influencers shines a light on its covert activities.

rows.title: Are pharmacy benefit managers driving up drug prices? (Update)
rows.standfirst: A group of obscure yet powerful players in the prescription drug industry are under the microscope. On Tuesday, at a Senate hearing in D.C., the head of pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk blamed the health insurance industry and pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, for allegedly making products like the weight loss drug Ozempic way more expensive in the U.S. than it is in other countries. A few days before that, the Federal Trade Commission sued three of the country's largest PBMs for allegedly using unfair tactics to artificially inflate the price of insulin.

rows.title: Inside the economic minds of the VP candidates
rows.standfirst: Next week, JD Vance and Tim Walz will face off in the only confirmed vice presidential debate ahead of the election. As voters look ahead to what their economic policies might be, we look back to see what they have said and done, and how it turned out.

rows.title: Without immigrants, America's job growth would have stalled
rows.standfirst: The share of Americans who are in the workforce today is the highest it's been in decades.

rows.title: California’s first plastic bag ban made things worse. Now it’s trying again
rows.standfirst: California and other states — and some cities — have learned a lesson: Bans on plastic bags don’t always go as planned. In fact, California's original ban made things worse.

frame: Up to15 visible Business-archive cards at four fixed weekly endpoints, restricted to each block; not a full-publication census
